item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Florida carried out its 20th execution of 2026 on Thursday, surpassing the state's modern-era record for most capital punishments in a single year. Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, was pronounced dead by lethal injection at Florida State Prison in Raiford at 6:19 p.m., according to North Escambia reporting. Overton had been sentenced to death for the…
item.content:encoded:
Florida carried out its 20th execution of 2026 on Thursday, surpassing the state's modern-era record for most capital punishments in a single year. Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, was pronounced dead by lethal injection at Florida State Prison in Raiford at 6:19 p.m., according to North Escambia reporting.

Overton had been sentenced to death for the murder of a Tavernier couple more than three decades ago. The execution marks a significant milestone in Florida's criminal justice system and reflects the state's accelerated pace of capital punishment this year.

The Escambia County School Board has officially approved a resolution honoring former band director William E. Slayton by naming the band building at Tate High School the "Bill Slayton Band Hall."

Slayton's decades of leadership and influence on the Tate High music program earned him recognition from the school district. The naming recognizes his contributions to music education and his impact on generations of students who passed through the program.

The resolution was approved at a recent school board meeting, making the honor official. The Bill Slayton Band Hall will serve as a lasting tribute to Slayton's legacy at Tate High School.

item.content:encoded:
Ascension Sacred Heart has introduced a portable brain MRI scanner to Pensacola, aiming to cut down on diagnostic delays for stroke patients and reduce emergency room wait times, according to reporting from WKRG-TV 5.

The mobile imaging technology allows emergency teams to perform brain scans more quickly than traditional MRI equipment, which is critical in stroke care where every minute counts. Getting patients diagnosed faster can determine whether they qualify for time-sensitive treatments that minimize brain damage.

The move reflects a broader trend among major health systems to bring advanced imaging closer to patients in emergency settings. For Pensacola's medical community, the portable MRI represents an upgrade in stroke response capabilities at one of the region's largest hospital operators.

item.content:encoded: Ascension Sacred Heart has brought a portable brain MRI machine to Pensacola, the first of its kind in Northwest Florida, according to WKRG News 5. The device is designed to ease bottlenecks in one of the hospital's busiest departments. "We have a busy stroke center. We have MRIs ordered every day; it could be as many as 50 to 60 a day," Sacred Heart neurologist Terry Neill told the station. The portable unit allows the hospital to handle diagnostic imaging more quickly, potentially reducing wait times for patients who may be experiencing acute neurological events like stroke. The addition is part of Ascension Sacred Heart's effort to expand diagnostic capacity and improve patient care delivery in the Pensacola market.

item.title: Senate Passes Bipartisan Bill Banning Disability Discrimination in Organ Transplants
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: The U.S. Senate has unanimously passed legislation aimed at preventing people with disabilities from being denied life-saving organ transplants based solely on their disability status. Senator Ashley Moody, a Florida Republican, brought the Charlotte Woodward Organ Transplant Discrimination Prevention Act to the Senate floor Wednesday, where it…
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Senate has unanimously passed legislation aimed at preventing people with disabilities from being denied life-saving organ transplants based solely on their disability status. Senator Ashley Moody, a Florida Republican, brought the Charlotte Woodward Organ Transplant Discrimination Prevention Act to the Senate floor Wednesday, where it passed without objection.

The bill is named after Charlotte Woodward, a woman with Down syndrome who received a heart transplant 14 years ago. According to the National Down Syndrome Society, discrimination in transplant decisions remains a documented problem: only 52 percent of people with disabilities who requested a referral to a transplant specialist actually received one. The society also reports that nearly half of pediatric transplant centers view intellectual disabilities as a negative factor when considering transplant candidates.

"It's hard to believe that in America, in 2026, a person could be denied consideration for a lifesaving organ transplant simply because they have a disability," Moody said in a statement. The legislation had previously passed the House and now heads to President Biden's desk. Moody was joined in sponsoring the bill by Senator Maggie Hassan, a New Hampshire Democrat, along with House sponsors Kat Cammack and Debbie Dingell.

item.title: Pensacola Beach Lifeguard Tryouts Set for December
item.dc:creator: newsroom

The positions offer a starting salary of $19.76 per hour and come with paid training for successful candidates. Applicants must meet several physical and…
item.content:encoded:
The Pensacola Beach Lifeguards are recruiting and will host tryouts on Saturday, December 12 and December 19 at 9 a.m. at the University of West Florida Aquatic Center on University Parkway. The positions offer a starting salary of $19.76 per hour and come with paid training for successful candidates.

Applicants must meet several physical and eligibility requirements. Candidates need to swim 550 yards in a pool within 10 minutes, run 1.5 miles on a track in 15 minutes or less, be at least 16 years old, and possess a valid driver's license. Interested individuals should arrive at least 15 minutes early and bring all relevant certifications to the tryout.

Those who pass the physical tests within the allotted time and satisfy all other requirements will advance to an interview stage. Hired applicants will receive paid training before starting the job. For more information, contact the Pensacola Beach Lifeguards directly.

item.title: AAA Warns Parents: That Electric Dirt Bike on Your Child's Christmas List May Not Be Street Legal
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: TAMPA, Fla. — Electric bikes and scooters are expected to be popular holiday gifts this year, but AAA is warning Florida families that some of the most powerful models may not be legal to operate on public roads. The organization has released a free E-Bike Holiday Gift Guide to help shoppers understand the differences between electric bicycles,…
item.content:encoded:
TAMPA, Fla. — Electric bikes and scooters are expected to be popular holiday gifts this year, but AAA is warning Florida families that some of the most powerful models may not be legal to operate on public roads.

The organization has released a free E-Bike Holiday Gift Guide to help shoppers understand the differences between electric bicycles, scooters and higher-powered electric motorcycles.

AAA spokesman Mark Jenkins says parents should pay particularly close attention when a child asks for something resembling an electric dirt bike.

While the devices may be marketed alongside traditional e-bikes, their speed, power and operating requirements can be very different.

Under Florida law, an electric bicycle must have operable pedals and an electric motor producing less than 750 watts.

Depending on its classification, motor assistance must stop at either 20 or 28 miles per hour.

More powerful electric devices may fall under motor vehicle regulations rather than bicycle laws.

That can affect whether the vehicle is permitted on public roads and whether the rider needs a driver's license or registration.

AAA is also encouraging families to purchase appropriate protective equipment.

Jenkins warns that not every helmet provides the same level of protection.

Traditional bicycle helmets are designed for lower-speed riding. Higher-speed electric bicycles may require helmets offering greater protection, while motorcycle-capable devices call for motorcycle-rated equipment.

AAA's guide also encourages shoppers to examine battery systems, braking performance, visibility and warranty support.

Buyers should be cautious of devices with unclear speed ratings or models advertised as capable of being unlocked to exceed their listed limits.

The free guide is available at sm.aaa/EBikeGiftGuide.

AAA recommends researching the device's legal classification and safety requirements before making a purchase.

item.title: Sen. Rick Scott's Bipartisan Lobbying Ban Blocked in Senate
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: U.S. Senator Rick Scott took to the Senate floor Wednesday to push for passage of the Banning Lobbying and Safeguarding Trust (BLAST) Act, a bipartisan measure co-sponsored with Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren that would impose a lifetime lobbying ban on former members of Congress. The effort stalled when North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis…
item.content:encoded:
U.S. Senator Rick Scott took to the Senate floor Wednesday to push for passage of the Banning Lobbying and Safeguarding Trust (BLAST) Act, a bipartisan measure co-sponsored with Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren that would impose a lifetime lobbying ban on former members of Congress. The effort stalled when North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis blocked immediate passage.

The BLAST Act, introduced in May, would prohibit former lawmakers from registering as lobbyists or making lobbying contacts on behalf of private interests, regardless of registration status. The bill also targets "shadow lobbying"—compensated lobbying activities that don't involve formal registration or direct contact. Violations could result in up to five years in prison and civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation.

Scott, a Florida Republican, framed the measure as part of his broader anti-corruption agenda. "When members of Congress go from elected office to lobbying, our jobs stop looking like public service and feel more like self-service," Scott said in a statement. He vowed to continue pushing the legislation despite the setback, citing it as essential to restoring public trust in Washington. The BLAST Act represents Scott's latest effort to reform congressional practices, following previous campaigns for term limits, elimination of taxpayer-funded Congressional pensions, and "No Budget, No Pay" legislation.

item.title: Free recovery fair Saturday helps Isaias survivors navigate FEMA, insurance claims
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Years after Hurricane Isaias, Pensacola survivors still struggling with rebuilding will have a chance to get hands-on help this weekend. A free resource fair Saturday at Pensacola State College will connect families with experts who can assist with FEMA applications and appeals, insurance claims, and other recovery obstacles that many disaster…
item.content:encoded:
Years after Hurricane Isaias, Pensacola survivors still struggling with rebuilding will have a chance to get hands-on help this weekend. A free resource fair Saturday at Pensacola State College will connect families with experts who can assist with FEMA applications and appeals, insurance claims, and other recovery obstacles that many disaster victims face long after the storm passes.

Hosted by Rebuild: The National Disaster Survivors Association, the event runs from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. at the college's Student Center (Building 5) on College Boulevard. More than a dozen organizations will be on-site, including the Florida Division of Emergency Management, ClaimsReady, Legal Services of North Florida, and others. The fair will also offer free childcare and meals — the Jordan Valley Mediterranean food truck will provide lunch to the first 100 attendees at no cost.

"Surviving the storm is just the beginning," said Devan Cheaves, Rebuild's Florida organizer. "Families shouldn't have to fight through FEMA paperwork, insurance disputes, and recovery delays alone." County Commissioner Lumon May and representatives from Commissioner Steve Stroberger's office are expected to attend. Media interested in covering the event can register at act.rebuild.us/isaias-fair.

item.title: Fill the Mayflower Returns Friday to Help Feed Northwest Florida Families
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: PENSACOLA, Fla. — One of Northwest Florida's biggest annual Thanksgiving food drives returns Friday, November 20, as Manna Food Bank and its community partners work to fill a Mayflower moving truck with donations for families in need. The annual Fill the Mayflower Food Drive will take place from 5 a.m. until 6 p.m. Friday in the Dillard's parking…
item.content:encoded:
PENSACOLA, Fla. — One of Northwest Florida's biggest annual Thanksgiving food drives returns Friday, November 20, as Manna Food Bank and its community partners work to fill a Mayflower moving truck with donations for families in need.

The annual Fill the Mayflower Food Drive will take place from 5 a.m. until 6 p.m. Friday in the Dillard's parking lot at Cordova Mall, 5100 North Ninth Avenue in Pensacola.

The collection site will be located between BJ's Restaurant & Brewhouse and Regions Bank.

The event is presented by Coastal Moving & Storage, with support from NewsRadio 92.3, Cat Country 98.7, WEAR ABC 3 and Cordova Mall.

Organizers are asking residents to donate nutritious, nonperishable food items or make financial contributions.

The food will help Manna provide assistance to children, families, senior citizens, veterans and other residents experiencing food insecurity throughout Escambia and Santa Rosa counties.

Manna Executive Director DeDe Flounlacker says the donations collected during Fill the Mayflower will help feed thousands of Northwest Florida residents in the months ahead.

What Should You Donate?

Manna says its most-needed items include:

  • Canned fruit packed in 100-percent juice

  • Canned mixed vegetables and tomatoes

  • Canned tuna or chicken

  • Microwaveable meals

  • Individual packets of oatmeal

  • Peanut butter

Donations must be unopened, commercially packaged and nonperishable.

Manna cannot accept homemade food, refrigerated items, opened containers or damaged and unlabeled cans.

You Don't Even Have to Get Out of Your Car

Organizers have designed the event to make donating as convenient as possible.

Drivers can pull up to the Mayflower truck, where volunteers will unload food donations directly from their vehicles.

Cash, checks and credit or debit card contributions will also be accepted.

According to Manna, a $25 donation can provide five days of food assistance for a child, while $50 can supply 30 meals for a senior citizen.

The organization says all contributions remain in the local community.

Manna reports helping more than 71,000 people in 2025, demonstrating the continuing demand for food assistance throughout Northwest Florida.

Residents unable to attend Friday can also contribute online through Manna Food Bank's website.

With Thanksgiving approaching, organizers hope the community will turn out to help fill the truck and provide food for neighbors who need it most.

item.title: Baptist Health Care Foundation Honors Community Supporters at Annual Celebration
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: PENSACOLA, Fla. — Baptist Health Care celebrated the people helping advance its mission Wednesday evening during the Baptist Health Care Foundation's annual gathering at the Pensacola Yacht Club. The event recognized physicians, volunteers, employees and longtime supporters whose contributions have helped the organization serve Northwest Florida.…
item.content:encoded:
PENSACOLA, Fla. — Baptist Health Care celebrated the people helping advance its mission Wednesday evening during the Baptist Health Care Foundation's annual gathering at the Pensacola Yacht Club.

The event recognized physicians, volunteers, employees and longtime supporters whose contributions have helped the organization serve Northwest Florida.

Brett Aldridge, Baptist Health Care's chief operating officer, told NewsRadio 92.3 that the annual celebration is an opportunity to recognize individuals who demonstrate the organization's values through their work and generosity.

The foundation plays an important role in supporting programs and services that might otherwise be difficult to provide.

Among those efforts are cancer care programs, mammograms for women who cannot afford them, and purchases of medical equipment.

Aldridge explained that the foundation allows community members to contribute their time and financial resources toward improving health care throughout the region.

The gathering also comes as Baptist Health Care celebrates 75 years of serving the Pensacola community.

Aldridge reflected on the organization's beginnings, when local residents gathered at a physician's home to discuss the need for better health care.

That community-driven beginning, he said, continues to shape Baptist's mission today.

Baptist Health Care is also preparing for a leadership transition.

Current President and CEO Mark Faulkner plans to retire June 30, 2027. Aldridge, a Pensacola native, has been selected to succeed him beginning July 1.

The foundation's annual celebration highlighted the importance of community involvement as the organization looks toward its next chapter.
